axes.brief:
Elected cabinets have repeatedly changed through competitive elections; constitutional courts, parliamentary opposition and confidence votes constrain the prime minister. The hereditary king remains a separate, influential head of state.
Focused six-question reassessment: Elected cabinets and confidence checks coexist with royal institutions. Bounded emergency measures are more constrained than a unilateral head-of-government law power, and parliamentary initiatives rather than general citizen-triggered law votes are the institutional baseline.
axes.counterEvidence:
Royal appointments, strict citizenship and candidate qualifications limit participation. Electoral Commission party restrictions are not unilateral exclusions by the governing leadership; prime-minister powers must not be confused with royal prerogatives.
The owner-defined broader axis includes lawful delegation and direct public control; a lower numerical placement is not a regime classification. Six exact responses and response strengths remain inferred. Retained source access dates are not refreshed unless a source was actually revisited. Unchanged answers and other axes were not re-audited. Elected cabinets and confidence checks coexist with royal institutions. Bounded emergency measures are more constrained than a unilateral head-of-government law power, and parliamentary initiatives rather than general citizen-triggered law votes are the institutional baseline.
